t: TraceDraw ヘルプへようこそ
h: このヘルプの構成 TraceDraw の中でヘルプを見る 最初に読むページ
x: TraceDraw ヘルプへようこそ TraceDraw は無料のオープンソースのベクター描画プログラムです。どのサイズでも鮮明なままの図形、線、テキストで、イラスト、ロゴ、図表、レイアウト、印刷物を描き、ビットマップと組み合わせることができます。同じプログラムが Windows、 macOS、Linux と Web ブラウザーで動きます。 このヘルプでは、TraceDraw での作業の手順と、各ダイアログボックス、パネル、ツールの働きを説明します。 このヘルプの構成 左側の目次は作業の流れに沿っています。 はじめに では、ワークスペース、新しい図面、開くことと保存を紹介します。 線、図形、アウトライン、オブジェクト、シンボル、レイヤー、 カラー、塗りつぶし、透明度 では、オブジェクトの描画と配置を扱います。 特殊効果、テキスト、テンプレートとスタイル、 ページとレイアウト、ビットマップ では、残りの描画作業を扱います。 印刷、Web グラフィック、ファイル形式 では、作品を TraceDraw から書き出す方法を扱います。 カスタマイズと自動化 ではオプション、ワークスペース、スクリプト、AI 機能を扱い、リファレンス ではすべてのメニューコマンド、ツール、パネル、キーボードショートカットを一覧します。 検索 タブではページに含まれる任意の語でページを探せます。上部の言語一覧では同じページを別の言語で読めます。 TraceDraw の中でヘルプを見る F1 キーを押すと、目の前にあるもののページが開きます。開いているダイアログボックス、なければ表示中のパネル、それもなければアクティブなツールです。 ダイアログボックスやオプションページの下にある ? ボタンをクリックすると、そのページが開きます。 ヘルプ > ヘルプトピック を選ぶと、このページが開きます。 ヒント パネルは作業中のアクティブなツールを説明し、その 詳細 リンクはここにあるツールのページを開きます。 ヒント を参照してください。 ページは Web ブラウザーで、TraceDraw に設定された言語で開きます。 最初に読むページ TraceDraw を初めて使う場合は、ワークスペース、次に 図面の作成 と 線と曲線の描画 を読んでください。

s: TraceDraw ヘルプへようこそ
h: プログラム内で新機能を見る 最近のバージョンの主な新機能
x: 新機能 TraceDraw の各バージョンでは機能と修正が加わります。このページでは、変更点を知る方法と、最近のバージョンの主な新機能を紹介します。 プログラム内で新機能を見る ヘルプ > 新機能 を選ぶと、このバージョンのニュースが載ったウェルカム画面の新機能ページが開きます。 ヘルプ > 新機能をハイライト をオンにすると、このバージョンの新しいものがメニューで示されます。新しいコマンドの末尾、そこへ通じるサブメニューの矢印の横、新しいコマンドを含むメニューのタイトルの上に小さな点が付きます。コマンドをオフにすると印は消え、TraceDraw を次に起動したときにはコマンドは再びオフになっています。 各バージョンの変更点の完全な一覧は、プロジェクトの 変更履歴 にあります。 最近のバージョンの主な新機能 お使いの言語でヘルプ。 すべての ? ボタンと F1 キーで、目の前のダイアログボックス、パネル、ツールについてのこのヘルプのページが、 TraceDraw に設定された言語で開きます。 ドキュメントのプロパティ。 ファイル > ドキュメントのプロパティ は図面の言語、タイトル、件名、作成者、著作権、タグ、メモ、評価を、図面の内容の完全なレポートとともに保持します。 ドキュメントのプロパティ を参照。 カラーマネジメント。 ツール > カラーマネージメント で図面のプロファイルと新しい図面の既定値を設定し、開くファイルや読み込むファイルの方針を決めます。 カラーマネジメント を参照。 バーコードと QR コード。 3 ステップのウィザードでバーコードを配置でき、 QR コードは プロパティ パネルで編集できるライブオブジェクトです。 バーコードと QR コード を参照。 効果。 効果 メニューに効果のパネルがまとまりました。ブレンドは一定の間隔でパスに沿わせたり、色を時計回りや反時計回りに回したりできます。ブレンド を参照。 パス上のテキスト には、向き、配置、距離、オフセットの独自の設定があります。テキストの追加と編集 を参照。 フォントマネージャー はインストール済みのフォント、フォルダー、お気に入り、コレクションを整理します。 フォントとグリフ を参照。

t: TraceDraw について、および更新
s: TraceDraw ヘルプへようこそ
h: バージョン情報ボックス 更新の確認 自動確認 ウェルカム画面 コミュニティとサポート
x: TraceDraw について、および更新 TraceDraw は無料でオープンソースです。このページでは、使っているバージョンの確認方法、新しいバージョンの入手方法、助けを求める場所を説明します。 バージョン情報ボックス ヘルプ > TraceDrawについて を選ぶと、実行中のバージョン、作者、ライセンス、ソースコードへのリンク、プログラムの構成要素が表示されます。 閉じる、Enter または Esc で閉じます。  更新の確認 デスクトップ版の TraceDraw は、新しいバージョンが公開されたときに知らせることができます。 今すぐ確認するには: ヘルプ > アップデート を選びます。 TraceDraw はプロジェクトのリリースページに最新バージョンを問い合わせ、お使いのバージョンより新しいかどうかを知らせます。テスト版とナイトリービルドが提示されることはありません。 新しいバージョンがある場合は、操作を選びます。 ダウンロード は、お使いのシステム用のファイルのダウンロードを開きます (Windows ではインストーラーまたはポータブルアーカイブ、Mac ではプロセッサーに合ったディスクイメージ、Linux では AppImage またはアーカイブ)。インストールはシステムのインストーラーが行います。 リリースノート は、そのバージョンの変更点の一覧を開きます。 このバージョンをスキップ は、そのバージョンを今後提示しません。 閉じる はボックスを閉じます。 TraceDraw が Linux の AppImage として動いているときは、ボックスに インストール も表示されることがあります。新しい AppImage を実行中のものの隣にダウンロードし、ダウンロードが完全で正規のものかを確認して、古いファイルと置き換えます。新しいバージョンは次に TraceDraw を開いたときに起動します。確認できない点があれば、古いファイルはそのまま残り、ボックスが理由を示します。 確認に失敗した場合 (インターネット接続がない場合など) は、ボックスがそれを知らせ、リリースページを提示します。  自動確認 ツール > オプション > グローバル の 全般 ページには、起動時に更新を確認する設定があります。最初はオンになっており、TraceDraw は 1 日に 1 回起動時に静かに確認し、スキップしていない新しいバージョンが出たときだけ知らせます。 注: ブラウザー版は常に最新です。そこでは ヘルプ > アップデート がリリースページを開きます。 ウェルカム画面 ウェルカム画面は TraceDraw の起動時に最初に表示されるタブです。ここから図面を作成したり、最近使った図面 (それぞれサムネイル付き。 リストをクリア で一覧を消去) を開いたり、テンプレートから始めたり、ニュースを読んだり、学習資料を探したりできます。 ヘルプ > ようこそ画面 を選ぶと再び表示されます。 ヘルプ > ビデオチュートリアル、クイックスタートガイド、 ユーザーガイド はその学習ページを、新機能 はニュースを開きます。 コミュニティとサポート ヘルプ > コミュニティ はプロジェクトのディスカッションフォーラムを開きます。質問したり、アイデアを共有したりできます。 ヘルプ > サポート は問題の追跡システムを開きます。問題を報告できます。 ヘルプ > メッセージ設定 は TraceDraw のメッセージを設定するオプションを開きます。
はじめに これらのページでは TraceDraw を紹介します。ウィンドウの各部、図面の作成、開き方と保存、図面内の移動と作業の取り消し、描画中にヘルプを見つける場所を説明します。 TraceDraw は Windows、macOS、Linux で動き、何もインストールせずに Web ブラウザーでも動きます。どちらも同じプログラムで、ブラウザー版のわずかな違いは ブラウザー版 で説明します。

x: ワークスペース TraceDraw のウィンドウには、図面と、それを作業するのに必要なものがすべて入っています。このページではその各部の名前を紹介し、このヘルプのほかのページを理解しやすくします。 ウィンドウの各部 上から下へ、左から右へ: メニューバー には、ファイル、編集、表示、レイアウト、オブジェクト、効果、ビットマップ、テキスト、表、ツール、ウィンドウ、ヘルプ の各メニューに、すべてのコマンドがあります。各コマンドの横にはショートカットが表示されます。図面を開いていないときは、ファイル、ツール、ウィンドウ、ヘルプ だけが表示されます。メニューコマンド のページにすべてのコマンドが一覧されています。 標準ツールバー には、よく使うコマンドがあります (下記を参照)。 プロパティバー には、今行っている操作の設定が表示されます。 ドキュメントタブ は、開いている図面ごとに一つのタブを表示します。 左側の ツールボックス には、ツールがあります。 定規 は、描画ウィンドウの上と左に沿って並びます。 描画ウィンドウ は、ページとその周りのデスクトップを表示します。 パネル は右側にあります。 カラーパレット は下に沿って並びます。 一番下の ステータスバー は、使用中のツールと選択範囲を説明します。 標準ツールバー 標準ツールバーには、グループごとに次のものがあります: 新規、開く (矢印は最近使った図面を一覧します)、保存、印刷。 切り取り、コピー、貼り付け。 元に戻す、やり直し。矢印は操作の段階を一覧するので、段階を選んで複数の操作を一度に元に戻したりやり直したりできます。 インポート、エクスポート、PDF に発行。 ズームボックス: ズームレベルを入力して Enter を押すか、一覧を開いて、選択範囲、すべてのオブジェクト、ページ、ページの幅または高さに合わせたズームや、10% から 1600% のレベルを選びます。その後に全画面プレビュー。 定規を表示、グリッドを表示、ガイドラインを表示。オンの間は押された状態で表示されます。 スナップをオフ (Alt+Q) と、スナップ先の一覧。 オプション。オプションのページの一覧を開きます。 起動: フォントマネージャー、ようこそ画面、カラーマネジメント。 ボタンにポインターを合わせると、その名前、ショートカット、機能が表示されます。 プロパティバー プロパティバーは操作に応じて変わります。何も選択せずに 選択 ツールを使っているときは、ページサイズと向き、図面単位、微調整の距離が表示されます。オブジェクトを選択していると、その位置、サイズ、拡大率、回転、反転ボタンが表示され、続いてその種類のオブジェクトの設定が表示されます。各ツールは独自の設定を追加します。これはツールのページで説明しています。 数値フィールドには、10+5 のような計算式や、1 in のような別の単位の値を入力でき、図面単位に変換されます。 ツールボックスとフライアウト ツールボックスには、ツールのグループごとに一つのボタンがあります。角に小さな矢印があるボタンには フライアウト、つまり関連するツールの一覧があります。フライアウトを開くには、矢印をクリックするか、ボタンを右クリックするか、ボタンを長押しします。ボタンには、そのグループで最後に使ったツールが表示されます。ツールにポインターを合わせると、その名前、ショートカット、機能が表示されます。 一部のボタンはダブルクリックでショートカット操作になります: 選択 はすべてのオブジェクトを選択し、ズーム はすべてのオブジェクトに合わせてズームし、長方形 はページと同じサイズの長方形を追加します。 ツールボックスの末尾の + ボタンは、各グループを表示または非表示にするチェックボックス付きでグループを一覧し、ツールボックスをリセットすることもできます。ツールボックス のページにすべてのツールが一覧されています。 パネル パネルには、作業中に開いたままにしておく設定が入っています。たとえば最初に開いている プロパティ、オブジェクト、ヒント です。開いているパネルは右側に縦に並ぶタブになります。タブをクリックするとそのパネルが前面に来ます。前面にあるタブをクリックするとパネルが折りたたまれます。ほかのパネルは ウィンドウ > パネル から、またはショートカットで開きます。タブの下の + でもパネルを追加できます。各パネルのタイトルバーには、折りたたみボタンと閉じるボタンがあります。パネル のページにすべてのパネルが一覧されています。 描画ウィンドウ ページはデスクトップの上にあります。デスクトップはページの周りの領域で、ここにもオブジェクトを置いておけます。図面の下には次のものがあります: ページナビゲーター: 前にページを挿入、最初のページ、前のページ、ページ番号、次のページ、最後のページ、後ろにページを挿入。 ページごとのタブ (クリックでそのページに移動、ダブルクリックで名前を変更)。 水平スクロールバー。ページタブとスクロールバーの間の点線の区切りをドラッグすると、両者の幅を配分できます。 スクロールバーの間の角にある ナビゲーター ボタンは、押している間ページのサムネイルを表示します。サムネイル上でポインターを動かすと表示位置が移動します。選択 ツールでページの境界をダブルクリックすると、ページサイズのオプションが開きます。 カラーパレット ステータスバーには、使用中のツールのヒント、何をどのレイヤーで選択しているか、選択範囲の塗りつぶしとアウトラインが表示されます。塗りつぶしまたはアウトラインの部分をダブルクリックすると変更できます。ステータスバー のページで各部を説明しています。 バーの配置 ツールボックス、カラーパレット、標準ツールバー、プロパティバー、ステータスバーは移動できます: バーを点線のつまみでウィンドウの別の端へドラッグするか、端から離してフローティングにします。つまみを右クリックすると、バーを固定したり位置をリセットしたりできます。バーを表示または非表示にするには ウィンドウ > ツールバー を使います。配置全体をワークスペースとして保存することもできます。ワークスペース を参照してください。 複数の図面での作業 開いている図面にはそれぞれ定規の上に専用のタブがあり、名前と、保存していない変更がある間は * が表示されます。最後のタブの後ろのタブは新しい図面を作成します。各図面は、ページ、元に戻す履歴、選択範囲、ズーム、単位をそれぞれ独自に保持します。 ウィンドウ > 重ねて表示、上下に並べて表示、左右に並べて表示 は、すべての図面をそれぞれ専用のウィンドウに表示します。ウィンドウを統合 でタブに戻ります。新しいウィンドウ は同じ図面の 2 つ目のウィンドウを開きます。たとえば二つのページや二つのズームレベルを同時に見るのに使います。一方のウィンドウでの編集は、すべてのウィンドウに表示されます。 インターフェイスのサイズ メニューやボタンが小さすぎる、または大きすぎる場合は、ツール > オプション > カスタマイズ を選び、外観 ページでインターフェイスのサイズを設定します。インターフェイスのサイズで図面のサイズが変わることはありません。カスタマイズのオプション を参照してください。

x: 図面を作成する どの図面も、ページサイズ、ページ数、カラーモード、解像度を持って始まります。これらは 新しいドキュメントの作成 ダイアログボックスで選びます。 図面を作成するには ファイル > 新規作成 (Ctrl+N) を選ぶか、標準ツールバーの「新規」をクリックするか、最後のドキュメントタブの後ろの + をクリックするか、ようこそ画面の「新規ドキュメント」をクリックします。 新しいドキュメントの作成 ダイアログボックスで、以下に説明する値を設定します。 OK をクリックするか Enter を押します。 図面は専用のタブで開きます。ダイアログボックスは、次の図面のために設定した値を記憶します。  一般 名前 は図面の名前です。最初は次の Untitled-N になっています。 プリセット は、カラーモード、ページサイズ、単位、解像度を一度に設定します。プリセットは TraceDraw の既定 と 既定の CMYK (CMYK、A4、ミリメートル、300 dpi)、既定の RGB (RGB、A4、ミリメートル、300 dpi)、Web (RGB、1920 x 1080 ピクセル、72 dpi) です。これらの値のどれかを変えると、値が再びプリセットと一致しない限り、プリセットは カスタム と表示されます。 プリセットの横のボタンには プリセットを保存 と プリセットを削除 があります。前者は プリセット名 を尋ねて現在の値を一覧に追加し、後者は保存したプリセットを削除します。組み込みのプリセットは削除できません。 ページ数 は図面のページ数を 1 から 999 の範囲で設定します。各ページは「ページ N」という名前で、レイヤーを一つ持ちます。 基本カラー モード は、印刷用の CMYK か、画面用の RGB です。 サイズ ページ サイズ は用紙サイズ、またはカスタムを一覧します。サイズを選ぶと、現在の向きはそのまま保たれます。入力した幅と高さがどちらかの向きで用紙サイズと一致すると、その名前が選ばれます。 幅 と 高さ はページサイズを、幅の横の一覧で選んだ単位で設定します。その単位がプロパティバーの図面単位になります。 方向: 縦 または 横。 解像度 は dpi 単位です (最初は 300)。ピクセルに変換される効果と、ピクセル単位でのサイズ計測に使われます。1920 ピクセルは 300 dpi では 162.56 mm、72 dpi では 677.33 mm です。単位がピクセルのときに解像度を変えると、ページのピクセル単位のサイズが保たれます。 カラー設定 カラー設定 を開いて、図面の RGB プロファイル、CMYK プロファイル、グレースケール プロファイル と レンダリング インテント を選びます。最初は sRGB、組み込みの CMYK プロファイル、ドットゲイン 20% のグレースケール、相対的な色域を維持、になっています。カラーマネジメント を参照してください。 ダイアログボックスを省略する 次回からこのダイアログを表示しない にチェックを付けると、前回使った値で新しい図面がすぐに作成されます。ダイアログボックスを再び表示するには、ツール > オプション > TraceDraw の 全般 ページで対応する設定をオンにします。TraceDraw のオプション を参照してください。 そのほかの始め方 ファイル > テンプレートから新規作成 はテンプレートから始めます。テンプレート を参照してください。 ファイル > 開く は既存の図面を開きます。図面を開く、保存する を参照してください。

見つからないフォントについては、その名前を示します。テキストは似たフォントで表示され、フォント名は保たれるので、そのフォントがあるコンピューターでは元どおりに戻ります。 今後このメッセージを表示しない にチェックを付けると、これらのメッセージは表示されなくなります。ツール > オプション > グローバル の 警告 ページで再びオンにできます。 図面を保存する ファイル > 保存 (Ctrl+S) を選ぶと、図面をそのファイルに書き戻します。新しい図面や、TraceDraw が読み込みしかできない形式から開いた図面にはまだファイルがないので、保存すると 図面を保存 ダイアログボックスが開きます。 名前を付けて保存 ファイル > 名前を付けて保存 (Ctrl+Shift+S) は、図面を別の名前、別のフォルダー、または別の形式で保存します。  図面を新しい名前で保存するには: ファイルでは形式のバージョンで、新しい順に並びます。.cdr ファイルではファイルのバージョンで、27 から 14 までです。古いプログラムは、自分と同じかそれより古いバージョンしか開けません。選んだバージョンは図面に記憶されるので、次の保存では尋ねずにそのバージョンで書き込みます。 バージョン 16 以降の .cdr ファイルでは、カラープロファイルを埋め込む は図面の CMYK プロファイルをファイルに格納し、フォントを埋め込む はライセンスが許す場合にテキストで使うフォントを格納します。どちらの選択も次回のために記憶されます。 必要に応じて タイトル、件名、評価 を入力します (点灯している最後の星をもう一度クリックすると外れます)。これらは図面のプロパティで、ドキュメントのプロパティ にも表示されます。 保存 をクリックするか Enter を押します。ファイルが既にある場合は、置換 するかどうかを TraceDraw が尋ねます。 ダイアログボックスは、図面のフォルダー、なければ最後に保存したフォルダー、それもなければドキュメントフォルダーで開きます。 メモ: ブラウザー版では、保存はすべてダウンロードになります。ダイアログボックスは名前、種類、バージョン、プロパティを保持し、ブラウザーがファイルをダウンロードフォルダーに置きます。 h: 元に戻す、やり直す 元に戻すパネル ズーム ズームツール パン 表示
x: 元に戻す、ズーム、パン どの変更も元に戻せます。また、図面をどのズームレベルでも、どの位置からでも見られます。ズームとパンで図面が変わることはありません。 元に戻す、やり直す 編集 > 元に戻す (Ctrl+Z) は最後の変更を取り消し、やり直し (Ctrl+Shift+Z) はそれをもう一度行います。 標準ツールバーの「元に戻す」と「やり直し」の横の矢印は、操作の段階を一覧します。段階を選ぶと、そこまでのすべての変更を元に戻すか、やり直します。 繰り返し は、最後のコマンドをもう一度適用します。たとえば次に選んだオブジェクトに適用できます。 元に戻すパネル 元に戻す パネルは、図面のすべての変更を古い順に一覧します。段階をクリックすると、図面をその段階の直後の状態に戻します。後の段階をクリックすると、再び先に進みます。ウィンドウ > パネル から開きます。  ズーム マウスホイールを回すと、ポインターを中心にズームインまたはズームアウトします。 標準ツールバーのズームボックスを使います: レベルを入力するか、一覧から選ぶか (10% から 1600%)、選択範囲、すべてのオブジェクト、ページ、ページの幅、ページの高さに合わせてズームします。 表示 > ズームイン と ズームアウト は 1 段階ズームします。全体に合わせてズーム (F4) はすべてのオブジェクトを、ページに合わせてズーム (Shift+F4) はページを、選択範囲に合わせてズーム (Shift+F2) は選択範囲を表示します。 トラックパッドのピンチでズームできます。タッチスクリーンでは、どのツールでも 2 本指でパンとピンチができます。 ズームツール ズーム ツール (Z または F2) を選んでから: クリックすると、その位置を中心に 2 倍にズームインします。 Shift+クリックまたは右クリックすると、2 分の 1 にズームアウトします。 長方形をドラッグすると、その長方形がウィンドウいっぱいになるようにズームします。 ツールのボタンをダブルクリックすると、すべてのオブジェクトに合わせてズームします。 パン どのツールでも、マウスの中ボタンを押したままドラッグします。 パン ツール (H) を選んでドラッグします。 Ctrl+ホイールで上下に、Alt+ホイールで左右にスクロールします。 スクロールバーを使います。スクロールバーはページとその周囲 1 ページ分の範囲をカバーします。 スクロールバーの間の角にあるナビゲーターボタンを押したまま、ページのサムネイル上でポインターを動かします。 PgUp と PgDn で前のページと次のページに移動します。 ホイールでズームではなくスクロールするには、ツール > オプション > ツール の ズーム/パン ページでマウスホイールの動作を変更します。すると、ホイールでスクロール、Shift+ホイールで左右にスクロール、Ctrl+ホイールでズームになります。ツールのオプション を参照してください。 表示 表示 メニューでは、オブジェクトの描き方を選びます: ワイヤーフレーム はアウトラインだけを表示し、標準 と 拡張 は塗りつぶしと効果を描き、ピクセル は図面をエクスポートしたときのピクセルとして表示します。全画面プレビュー はページだけを画面に表示します。何かキーを押すと戻ります。選択範囲のみプレビュー は、そのプレビューを選択範囲に限定します。表示 メニューでは、定規、グリッド、ガイドライン、裁ち落とし、印刷可能領域の表示と非表示も切り替えます。定規、グリッド、ガイドライン を参照してください。

t: 図面を GitHub に保管する
h: 始める前に: トークン GitHub から図面を開く GitHub に図面を保存する GitHub が保存を拒否したとき 以前のバージョンを開く
x: 図面を GitHub に保管する TraceDraw は、デスクトップでもブラウザーでも、GitHub のリポジトリから図面を開き、コミットとして保存し直せます。保存するたびにリポジトリの履歴に一つのバージョンができ、後でそれを開き直せます。コマンドは ファイル > GitHub にあります。 始める前に: トークン 公開リポジトリはトークンなしで開けます。非公開のリポジトリを開いたり保存したりするには、GitHub でリポジトリのコンテンツに読み書きのアクセス権を持つ fine-grained personal access token を作成し、トークン フィールドに貼り付けます。 トークンは TraceDraw の実行中は保持されます。次回のために残すには このコンピューターにトークンを記憶する にチェックを付けます。この場合、トークンは環境設定に平文で保存されます (ブラウザーでは、そのブラウザーのストレージに保存されます)。ダイアログボックスは、最後に使ったリポジトリ、ブランチ、パスも記憶します。 GitHub から図面を開く ファイル > GitHub > GitHub から開く を選びます。 リポジトリ を owner/name の形式か、その github.com のアドレスで入力します。 ブランチ を入力します。空のままにすると main になります。 リポジトリ内のファイル のパスを入力します。例: art/logo.tdraw。 OK をクリックします。 図面はファイル名の付いた新しいタブで開きます。図面は、どこから来たか、どのバージョンだったかを記憶しています。  GitHub に図面を保存する GitHub から開いた図面は、保存 (Ctrl+S) でそのまま保存し直せます。どの図面でも、ファイル > GitHub > GitHub に保存 を選べます。 リポジトリ、ブランチ、パスを確認します。 何を変更したかを書いた コミットメッセージ を入力します (最初は "Update" とファイル名が入っています)。 OK をクリックします。 図面はフォントを含む .tdraw ファイルとして、そのブランチの新しいコミットとして保存されます。名前を付けて保存 は、これまでどおりコンピューター上にファイルを保存します。  GitHub が保存を拒否したとき 開いた後に GitHub 上でファイルが変更された場合や、そのパスに既にファイルがあり、図面がそこから開いたものでない場合、GitHub は保存を拒否し、ダイアログボックスにその旨が表示されます。別のパスかブランチに保存するか、先に新しいバージョンを開いてください。ダイアログボックスは、ほかの問題も説明します: トークンが拒否された、またはアクセス権がない、リクエストが多すぎる、リポジトリ、ブランチ、ファイルが存在しない、パスがフォルダーである、ファイルが図面ではない、図面が 100 MB より大きい、といった問題です。 以前のバージョンを開く GitHub から開いた図面で、ファイル > GitHub > 履歴 を選びます。ボックスには、そのファイルを変更したコミットが新しい順に、短い ID、日付、作成者、メッセージとともに一覧されます。一つを選んで「開く」をクリックすると、そのバージョンがファイル名とコミット名の付いた新しい図面として開きます。この図面は GitHub とは結び付いていません。
線、図形、アウトライン TraceDraw で描くものはすべて線と図形でできています。これらのページでは、それらを描くツール、ノードごとの形の変更、結合と切断、そして端を描くアウトラインの設定を説明します。 線と曲線は曲線フライアウトのツールで、長方形、楕円、多角形などの図形はそれぞれのツールで描きます。どのオブジェクトも、描いた後で シェイプ ツールで形を変えられます。

h: Freehand 2-Point Line Bezier Pen B-Spline Polyline 3-Point Curve Continuing a curve The property bar Editing curves afterwards
x: Drawing lines and curves A line in TraceDraw is a curve: a path made of segments that join at nodes. Segments can be straight or curved. A curve can be open, with two ends, or closed, when its end meets its start, and then it can be filled. The curve tools are in the Curve flyout of the toolbox. Every one of them draws a curve with the default fill and outline of new objects; change them afterwards in the Properties panel or with the color palette. Freehand The Freehand tool (F5) draws a line where you drag, like a pencil. Choose the Freehand tool. Drag on the page. Release the button to finish. TraceDraw follows the pointer and smooths the line when you release it. The smoothing (0 to 100, 50 at first) on the property bar sets how much: a higher value gives fewer nodes and a softer line. When you are zoomed in, the line keeps more detail. To draw a straight line with this tool, click where the line starts and click again where it ends. Hold Ctrl to keep the line to steps of 15 degrees. Esc drops the first click. 2-Point Line The 2-Point Line tool draws one straight segment: press where it starts and release where it ends, or click twice. Hold Ctrl to keep it to steps of 15 degrees. Bezier The Bezier tool draws precise curves node by node. Choose the Bezier tool. Click to place a corner node (a cusp), or drag to place a smooth node and pull out its handles, which set the direction and the bend of the curve. Go on placing nodes. Double-click or press Enter to finish. To close the curve, click its first node. Esc throws away the curve you are drawing. Hold Ctrl to place the next node in steps of 15 degrees from the last one, or to turn a handle in such steps. Every node snaps to what snapping is set to; see Snapping. Pen The Pen tool places nodes the same way as the Bezier tool: click for a corner node, drag for a smooth node, double-click or Enter to finish, click the first node to close. While the button is down, the handle follows the pointer, so you see the curve take shape. B-Spline The B-Spline tool draws smooth curves from control points, without handles. Click to place each control point. The curve follows the points, starting at the first and ending at the last, and always stays inside them. While you draw, the control points show as a dashed line. Double-click or press Enter to finish. Click the first point (once there are three) to close the curve into a smooth loop. The result is an ordinary curve; the control points are not kept. Polyline The Polyline tool draws straight segments one after the other: click to add each corner, and double-click or press Enter to finish. Hold Ctrl to keep each segment to steps of 15 degrees. 3-Point Curve The 3-Point Curve tool draws an arc through three points: Drag from where the curve starts to where it ends. Move the pointer to bend the curve, and click the point it passes through. Continuing a curve To add to an open curve, select it, then draw with the Freehand, 2-Point Line, Bezier, Pen, B-Spline or Polyline tool starting (or ending) on one of its end nodes. The new line becomes part of the curve: it runs on from that end; when it ends on the curve's other end, the curve closes; when it ends on an end of another part of the same curve, the two parts join. The pointer shows a node with a line going on from it when you are over an end node, and a ring when a click would close the curve. The curve keeps its look and stays selected, and the change is one undo step. Closed curves, several selected objects and objects inside groups are never continued. The distance that counts as "on the node" is set on the Curve tools page of the tool options; see Tool options. The property bar While a curve tool is active, the property bar shows the position, size, scale, angle and mirror buttons of the selection, its outline width, line style and start and end arrowheads, and a button that closes an open curve. The Freehand tool adds the smoothing. With nothing selected, it reminds you how to finish a curve. See Outlines for the outline settings. Editing curves afterwards Use the Shape tool to move, add and delete nodes, change their type and bend segments; see Shaping curves with the Shape tool.

h: Brush Strokes Modes Settings Painterly Brush Brushes and settings
x: Brush strokes and painterly brushes Brush strokes turn a line you draw into a filled shape with a varying width, like ink from a pen or a brush. Painterly brushes paint the outline of an object with marks of chalk, ink, watercolor and other media. Brush Strokes The Brush Strokes tool (I) draws strokes in one of five modes. The stroke is a filled object: it takes the current fill color (black when there is none) and no outline, and you edit it like any curve. To draw a brush stroke: Choose the Brush Strokes tool. Choose a mode and its settings on the property bar or in the Brush Strokes panel. Drag on the page. To turn existing curves into strokes, select them and click Apply to curve in the Brush Strokes panel.  Modes Calligraphic: a flat nib of the given width, held at the given angle (45 degrees at first). The stroke is thinnest where you move along the nib and widest across it. Preset: a stroke whose width follows a profile: taper both ends (at first), taper start, taper end, bulge, wave or flat. The width is the widest point. Brush: a preset profile with a rough, dry-brush edge. Expression: the width follows your speed as if it were pen pressure: slow strokes are wide. The pressure setting scales the effect. Sprayer: shapes (circles, squares, stars, hearts or leaves) placed along the line every spacing (8 mm at first), each between 70% and 100% of the width. Settings Width: 3 mm at first. Angle: the nib's angle, for Calligraphic. Smoothing: 0 to 100 (25 at first). Higher values smooth out wobbles. Pressure: for Expression (0.5 at first). Spacing: for Sprayer. Painterly Brush The Painterly Brush tool, in the same flyout, paints a line made of brush marks. The brushstroke is an ordinary curve with no fill: the Shape tool reshapes it, the outline color colors it, and the marks follow. To paint a stroke: Choose the Painterly Brush tool. Choose a brush, a size and a transparency on the property bar. Drag on the page. To paint the outline of existing objects, click them to select them, then pick a brush: their outlines are painted with it. Changing the size or the transparency changes their brushstrokes. Clear Brushstroke gives the selected objects their plain outline back. Brushes and settings Brush: dry media (Chalk, which is the first, Charcoal, Soft Pastel), wet media (Ink Wash, Watercolour, Dry Brush) and textures (Bristle, Fur, Spray, Speckle, Cloud, Silk Ribbon). Brush size: 0.1 to 200 mm, 5 mm at first. Transparency: 0 to 100%, 20% at first. Most brushes thin out towards both ends. The marks are laid the same way each time the stroke is drawn, exported or printed. With "Scale with object" on, the marks grow and shrink with the object. In SVG and PDF exports the marks become filled shapes with their transparency.

h: Shape Recognition Sketch
x: Sketching and shape recognition Two tools turn quick hand-drawn strokes into clean objects: the Shape Recognition tool recognizes the shape you meant, and the Sketch tool builds a smooth line from several strokes. Shape Recognition The Shape Recognition tool (Shift+S) turns a freehand stroke into the shape it looks like, as you drew it: a tilted rectangle stays tilted. Choose the Shape Recognition tool. Draw the shape in one stroke. A stroke whose ends come close together is taken as closed. Release the button. What you get: An open stroke that is nearly straight becomes a straight line; otherwise a smooth curve. A closed stroke with four corners near right angles becomes a rectangle. When it is nearly level, it comes out level. A closed, rounded stroke becomes an ellipse, level when nearly level and never tilted when nearly round. A closed stroke with three corners becomes a triangle, and one with four other corners a four-sided shape. Anything else becomes a smooth closed curve. The new object takes the default fill and outline and is selected. On the property bar, Shape recognition sets how readily strokes become shapes, and Smoothing how much the leftover curves are smoothed. Each is None, Lowest, Low, Medium (at first), High or Highest. With recognition at None, every stroke stays a curve. Sketch The Sketch tool (S) lets you build a line from several short strokes, as you would with a pencil. Choose the Sketch tool. Draw a stroke. It is smoothed and selected. Draw the next stroke starting near the end of the first. With Join on, it is added to the same curve. On the property bar, Join adds a stroke to the selected open curve when it starts close enough to its end; the distance beside it sets how close (5 mm at first). Smoothing sets how much each stroke is smoothed, from None to Highest.

h: Drawing with a box Rectangle Corners 3-Point Rectangle Ellipse 3-Point Ellipse The Corners panel
x: Drawing rectangles and ellipses Rectangles and ellipses stay rectangles and ellipses after you draw them: you can change their corners, turn an ellipse into a pie or an arc, and still resize them freely. To edit them node by node, convert them to curves with Object > Convert to Curves. Drawing with a box The Rectangle, Ellipse, polygon, star, spiral, graph paper, common shapes and action lines tools all draw by dragging a box. While you drag, the object itself follows the pointer, with the settings of the property bar. Hold Ctrl to draw a square, a circle or a regular shape. Hold Shift to draw from the center out. You can press or release it while dragging. The start and end points snap to what snapping is set to. The new object takes the default fill and outline (no fill and a thin black outline at first) and is selected. To change those defaults, see Object styles and defaults. Rectangle Choose the Rectangle tool (F6) and drag from one corner to the opposite one. Double-click the tool's button to draw a rectangle the size of the page; hold Shift while you double-click to frame the selection instead. Corners The property bar sets the corners of the selected rectangles, or of new ones when nothing is selected: The corner style: Round (a quarter circle), Scalloped (a quarter circle cut inwards) or Chamfered (a straight cut). The four sizes: top left, top right, bottom left and bottom right. The size is the radius, or for a chamfer how far from the corner the cut starts. A corner is at most half the shorter side. Edit corners together (the lock, on at first) gives all four the size you type in one. Relative corner scaling (on at first): the corners grow and shrink with the rectangle. Turned off, they keep their size when you resize the rectangle and stay round when you stretch it. You can also drag a corner node with the Shape tool to round all corners at once. 3-Point Rectangle The 3-Point Rectangle tool draws a rectangle at an angle: Drag to draw the base line, at any angle. Move the pointer to set the height and click. Ellipse Choose the Ellipse tool (F7) and drag a box. Hold Ctrl for a circle. On the property bar, choose Ellipse, Pie or Arc. For a pie or an arc, set the start and end angles (in degrees, counterclockwise from the right) and the direction. You can also drag the node of an ellipse with the Shape tool to make a pie (drag inside) or an arc (drag outside). 3-Point Ellipse The 3-Point Ellipse tool draws an ellipse at an angle: Drag to draw the center line of the ellipse, at any angle. Move the pointer to set the height and click. The Corners panel The Corners panel rounds, scallops or chamfers the corners of curves, which the rectangle settings cannot do. Open it from Window > Panels.  Select one or more objects. Rectangles, ellipses, polygons and text become curves when the corners are cut. Choose the Operation: Fillet (a round arc that touches both sides), Scallop (a notch, a quarter of a circle around the corner) or Chamfer (a straight cut). Set the Radius for a fillet or scallop (2 mm at first), or the Chamfer distance for a chamfer: the first distance along the side the path comes in on and the second along the side it leaves on. Equal distances keeps them the same. The result shows as a dashed outline on the drawing. Click Apply. A corner is a node where two segments meet at an angle; smooth nodes are not corners. With the Shape tool and some nodes selected, only those corners are cut. A corner whose sides are too short for the cut is skipped.

t: Drawing polygons, stars, spirals and other shapes
h: Polygon Star Spiral Common Shapes Action Lines Graph Paper
x: Drawing polygons, stars, spirals and other shapes These tools draw ready-made shapes by dragging a box. As with rectangles, hold Ctrl to keep the shape regular and Shift to draw from the center; see Drawing with a box. Polygon The Polygon tool (Y) draws a regular polygon. Set the number of points (3 to 500, 5 at first) on the property bar before or after drawing. The first corner is at the top center. Polygons are symmetric: when you move one node with the Shape tool, the matching nodes of every side move with it, so you can turn a pentagon into a flower in one drag. Star The Star tool draws a star. Its property bar starts with two buttons that choose what it draws: Star: a star with the given number of points (5 at first) and sharpness (0.5 at first; 0 makes a polygon, 1 the thinnest spikes). Complex star: a star whose sides cross, made by joining each point to one further on (9 points and sharpness 2 at first). Its middle stays empty. With some numbers of points it is made of several closed shapes, as six points give two triangles. Spiral The Spiral tool (A) draws a spiral, an open curve. On the property bar set the revolutions (1 to 100, 4 at first) and choose a symmetrical spiral, whose turns are evenly spaced, or a logarithmic one, whose turns grow further apart. Hold Ctrl to draw a round spiral. Common Shapes The Common Shapes tool draws ready-made shapes. Click the shape button on the property bar to choose one from five sets: Basic shapes: parallelogram, trapezoid, diamond, triangles, hexagon, octagon, plus, heart, lightning, crescent, ring, cylinder, cube, frame, teardrop, smiley face and no symbol. Arrows: in every direction, chevron, pentagon, notched, striped and bent arrows. Flowchart: process, decision, data, document, terminator, connector, storage and the other usual symbols. Banners: ribbons, waves, scroll, explosion, burst and pennant. Callouts: rectangle, rounded, oval, cloud and line callouts. Then drag a box. The shape becomes one curve with the default fill and outline. Parts that should look separate, such as the faces of a cube, are separate parts of the curve, and holes such as the middle of a ring stay holes whatever the fill. Action Lines The Action Lines tool draws speed lines in a comic-book style: a group of lines (2 to 500, 12 at first) that are parallel (at first) or radial. Their lengths vary, but the same box always gives the same lines. Graph Paper The Graph Paper tool (D) draws a grid of cells: a group of rectangles that fill the box exactly. Set the rows and columns (4 by 3 at first) on the property bar. Hold Ctrl for square cells. The default points, revolutions, rows and columns are also on the tool pages of the options; see Tool options.

t: Shaping curves with the Shape tool
h: Nodes and segments Selecting nodes Moving nodes and bending segments The property bar Aligning nodes Rectangles, ellipses, polygons and other objects
x: Shaping curves with the Shape tool The Shape tool (F10) edits the nodes and segments of a curve: you move nodes, bend segments, add and delete nodes and change how each node joins its segments. Nodes and segments Select a curve with the Shape tool. Its outline shows in the node color, its nodes as small markers, and the first node of each part of the curve as a slightly larger triangle. A selected node shows its control handles: dashed lines that end in an arrow at the control point. A node is one of three types: Cusp: the segments meet at an angle; each handle moves on its own. Smooth: the curve passes through without a corner; the two handles stay in line. Symmetrical: smooth, with both handles the same length. The pointer shows what a press would take: a small square over a node, a dot over a control handle, a wave over a segment. Selecting nodes Click a node to select it alone; Ctrl+click adds it or takes it out of the selection. Shift+click selects every node from the last selected one to the one you click. Drag a marquee around nodes. The property bar's selection mode chooses a rectangular or a freehand marquee. Tab and Shift+Tab select the next or previous node; Home and End the first or last. Ctrl+A, the select all nodes button, or a double-click on the tool's button selects every node. Moving nodes and bending segments Drag a node to move the selected nodes. Hold Ctrl to move only horizontally or vertically. Nodes snap like drawing points. Drag a segment to bend it: the point you grab follows the pointer while the nodes at its ends stay. A straight segment becomes curved. Drag a control handle to change the bend. The arrow keys nudge the selected nodes (Shift for a larger step, Ctrl for a smaller one). Double-click a segment to add a node there, a node to delete it. Click a segment to mark a spot, then press + to add a node there. Delete or - deletes the selected nodes; + adds a node in the middle of each segment that ends at them. With nodes selected, C switches them between cusp and smooth, S between smooth and symmetrical, and Y makes them symmetrical. With nodes selected, Ctrl+C copies the segments between them as new curves, Ctrl+X cuts them out, and Ctrl+D duplicates them. Right-click a node or segment for a menu of the commands below. The property bar Selection mode: rectangular or freehand marquee. Add node and Delete node. Join nodes joins two end nodes into one; Break curve splits the curve at the selected node. Convert to line and Convert to curve make the segment ending at the node straight or curved. Cusp, Smooth and Symmetrical set the node type. Reverse direction turns the curve round; Extend curve to close joins two selected end nodes with a straight segment; Extract subpath makes the part of the selected node a curve of its own; Close curve closes an open curve. Stretch and scale nodes and Rotate and skew nodes frame two or more selected nodes with handles: the corner handles scale (or rotate), the side handles stretch (or skew) only those nodes. Align nodes opens the Node Align dialog box (see below). Reflect horizontally and Reflect vertically: moving a node moves the selected nodes on the other side the mirrored way, so both sides of a shape change together. Elastic mode: the selected nodes move less the further they are from the one you drag, down to half as much for the furthest. Select all nodes. Reduce nodes removes nodes that are not needed, from the selected nodes or from the whole curve. Drag the curve smoothness slider to remove more nodes gradually. Aligning nodes To line up nodes: Select two or more nodes with the Shape tool. Click Align nodes on the property bar. In the Node Align dialog box, tick Align horizontal, Align vertical or both, and click OK. The selected nodes move onto a common horizontal or vertical line, or onto one point when both are ticked.  Rectangles, ellipses, polygons and other objects Drag a corner node of a rectangle to round every corner; Ctrl+drag (or click it first) to round that corner only. Drag the node of an ellipse inside it to make a pie, outside it to make an arc. Drag a node of a polygon or star: the matching nodes follow, so the shape stays symmetric. Dragging the points between the corners sharpens or twists a star. Double-click a rectangle, ellipse or polygon to turn it into a curve. Drag a corner of a picture to crop it: the picture goes into a frame whose nodes you can edit like a curve. With text, the Shape tool moves single characters; see Adding and editing text. The appearance of nodes and handles is set on the Nodes and Handles page of the options; see TraceDraw options.

h: Using a shaping brush Smooth Smear Twirl Attract and Repel Smudge Roughen
x: Smoothing, smearing and roughening outlines The shaping brushes of the Shape flyout reshape the outline of an object where you drag over it, like a sculptor's tool: Smooth, Smear, Twirl, Attract and Repel, Smudge and Roughen. Using a shaping brush Select a curve. Other objects are converted to curves first; with nothing selected, the object under the pointer is used. Choose the tool and set its Nib size (the radius of the brush, 10 mm at first) and its other settings on the property bar. Drag over the outline. The effect is strongest at the center of the nib and fades to nothing at its edge. Only the parts of the outline within reach change; open curves stay open and closed ones stay closed. Each drag is one undo step. The settings are kept for the next time. Smooth The Smooth tool removes wobbles and extra nodes where you drag. Rate (1 to 100%, 20% at first) sets how strongly. Smear The Smear tool (W) pulls the outline along with the pointer, as if you smeared wet paint. Pressure (1 to 100%, 100% at first) sets how far it moves. Twirl The Twirl tool turns the outline around the pointer into a swirl. Speed (1 to 100%, 50% at first) sets how fast it turns, and the direction buttons choose counterclockwise or clockwise; hold Alt or Shift while dragging to turn the other way. Holding the pointer still keeps turning. Attract and Repel The Attract and Repel tool pulls the nodes inside the nib towards the pointer, or pushes them away. Speed (1 to 100%, 50% at first) sets how fast; choose Attract or Repel on the property bar, or hold Alt or Shift while dragging to swap them. Holding the pointer still keeps going. Smudge The Smudge tool (V) smooths the outline slightly, then smears it, so it is pulled without kinks. Pressure (1 to 100%, 100% at first) sets how far. Roughen The Roughen tool (E) adds jagged spikes along the outline. Frequency (1 to 10 spikes per 10 mm, 5 at first) sets how many, and Spike size (2 mm at first) how tall. The spikes are straight, so they stay sharp.

h: Crop Knife Segment Delete Eraser
x: Cropping, cutting and erasing Four tools of the Crop flyout take parts of objects away: Crop, Knife, Segment Delete and Eraser. Each change is one undo step. Crop The Crop tool removes everything outside a rectangle. Select the objects to crop, or select nothing to crop every unlocked object on the page. Choose the Crop tool and drag the crop area. The drawing outside it is dimmed. Adjust the area: drag inside it to move it, drag one of its eight handles to resize it, or type its position and size on the property bar. Double-click inside the area, press Enter or click Crop on the property bar. To give up, press Esc, click outside the area, click Clear crop area, or choose another tool. What happens to each object: objects wholly inside stay as they are, and objects wholly outside are deleted; closed shapes are cut to the area, and open curves are cut where they cross its edge; text becomes curves first; bitmaps, tables and symbols are placed inside a frame of the area, so their content stays whole and can be taken out again (see Clip frames); groups are cropped member by member. Knife The Knife tool splits objects along a cut. Select the objects to cut, or select nothing to cut every visible object on the page. Choose the Knife tool and the kind of cut on the property bar: Two-point line (a straight cut that runs on across the objects) or Freehand (a cut that follows your drag). Drag across the objects. On the property bar, Split separates the pieces with a hairline gap, so they still meet, and Gap removes a band of the width you type. With Keep as one object, the pieces of each object stay one object made of several parts. Open curves are split where the cut crosses them. Pieces keep the fill, outline and transparency and are selected. Bitmaps, groups and text are not cut. Segment Delete The Segment Delete tool deletes the parts of outlines between the places where they cross other outlines or themselves, for example the bits of lines that stick out past a crossing. Click a part of an outline to delete it. Drag a rectangle to delete every part that lies wholly inside it, on all objects at once. Rectangles, ellipses and polygons become curves; a closed shape that loses a part opens, and an object with nothing left is deleted. Eraser The Eraser tool (X) rubs out parts of objects. Select the objects to erase, or select nothing to erase the object you start dragging on. Choose the Eraser tool. Set the thickness (6.35 mm at first) and the round or square nib on the property bar. Drag over the objects. A click erases one dot. Erased objects become curves; an object erased completely is deleted. Double-click an object with the tool to delete it whole. Bitmaps, groups and clip frames are not erased. The defaults of the eraser are on the Eraser page of the tool options; see Tool options.

t: Combining shapes: weld, trim and intersect
h: The target and the sources The operations The Shaping panel
x: Combining shapes: weld, trim and intersect Shaping builds new shapes from overlapping objects: join them into one, cut one with another, or keep only where they overlap. The commands are in Object > Shaping, on the property bar when two or more objects are selected, and in the Shaping panel. The target and the sources The last object you select is the target: it gives the result its fill, outline and transparency. The other selected objects are the sources. To choose the target, select the sources first, then Shift+click the target. The result goes on top of the active layer and is selected. Each operation is one undo step. When there is no result (for example two objects that do not overlap), nothing changes and the status bar says so. The operations Weld 2 objects one object covering all of them Trim 2 objects the target without what the sources cover Intersect 2 objects only the area all of them share Simplify 1 object each object without what the objects above it cover Front Minus Back 2 objects the front object without the ones behind it Back Minus Front 2 objects the back object without the ones in front of it Boundary 1 object an outline around the whole selection From the menu and the property bar, Weld removes the originals, Trim keeps the sources, Intersect keeps all of them, and Boundary keeps them all. The Shaping panel Open the Shaping panel from Object > Shaping > Shaping.  Click one of the seven picture buttons to choose the operation. The panel shows its name, a picture and what it does. For Weld, Trim and Intersect, choose what to keep: Leave original source object and Leave original target object. Each operation remembers its own choice. Select the objects, the target last. Click the button named after the operation. It stays pale until enough objects are selected, and a line says how many are needed. Related: Combine (Ctrl+L) makes several objects one curve without changing their shapes, and Break Apart splits a curve into its parts again. See Objects and layers.

h: To join curves
x: Joining curves The Join Curves panel closes the gaps between the ends of curves, for example lines that should meet at a corner but stop short of it. Open it with Object > Join Curves.  To join curves Select the curves. Open parts inside one curve are joined too. Choose how the ends are joined: Extend: both ends carry on in their directions until they meet, as a corner. When the directions never meet ahead of both ends, a straight line joins them. Chamfer: a straight line between the ends. Fillet: as Extend, then the corner is rounded with the radius (2 mm at first). Bezier curve: a smooth curve that leaves and arrives in the directions of the ends. Set the gap tolerance (5 mm at first). Ends further apart are not joined. Click Apply. The closest pair of ends is joined first, then the next, until no pair is left within the tolerance; the two ends of one part close it. The joined curve takes the place, fill and outline of the curve you selected last, and the other curves are removed. When no ends lie close enough, nothing changes and the status bar says so. You can also join two end nodes of one curve with the Shape tool; see Shaping curves with the Shape tool. Drawing from the end of a selected curve also continues it; see Continuing a curve.

h: Opening the outline settings Outline Pen settings Outline Color Variable Outline
x: Setting outlines The outline is the line drawn along the edge of an object. You set its color, width, style, corners, line ends and arrowheads in the Outline section of the Properties panel. Opening the outline settings The Outline Pen tool (F12) opens the Properties panel at the Outline section, then goes back to the Pick tool. Double-click the outline part of the status bar. Right-click a color of the palette to color the outline of the selection. Outline Pen settings Width: 0.2 mm for new objects. Hairline draws a line one screen or printer dot wide at every zoom. Paint: the outline can be painted like a fill: none, uniform color, gradient, pattern, texture or mesh. See Fills. Hairlines and arrowheads keep the plain outline color. Caps, the ends of open lines: Butt (at first), Round or Square. Corners: Miter (at first), Round or Bevel. Dash: Solid, Dashed, Dotted or Dash dot. The dashes grow with the width. Arrowheads, at the Start and the End of open lines, filled in the outline color. To make your own, draw it, select it and choose Object > Create > Arrowhead. The nib stretch (0.1 to 1) and nib angle make a calligraphic outline: thinner across the nib than along it, like a flat pen. Behind fill draws the outline under the fill, so only its outer half shows. Scale with object: the width grows and shrinks when you resize the object. To turn an outline into an object you can fill, choose Object > Convert Outline to Object (Ctrl+Shift+Q). The settings of new objects are explained in Object styles and defaults. Outline Color The Outline Color tool (Shift+F12) opens the Color panel to choose the outline color of the selection. See The Color panel. Variable Outline The Variable Outline tool, in the Shape flyout, makes an outline thicker or thinner along its length with width nodes. Select an object with an outline, such as a curve, a rectangle or an ellipse. An object with no outline gets a thin one. Choose the Variable Outline tool. Drag across the outline: a width node is added where you start, and the outline reaches to the pointer on both sides. Hold Alt as you start dragging to change only the side the pointer is on. Add more nodes the same way. Between nodes the width changes smoothly. To change a node, click it and type the Left width and Right width on the property bar (left is to the left of the path's direction). Delete node or Delete removes the selected node, and Clear variable outline gives back the plain outline.

h: Placing a dimension Parallel Horizontal or Vertical Angular Segment Dimension style Callout
x: Dimension lines and callouts Dimension lines show the size of things in a technical drawing: a length, a horizontal or vertical distance, an angle or the length of a segment. Callouts point at something with a leader line and a label. Both stay live: when you move, scale or turn them, they are measured and drawn again. Placing a dimension Every dimension is placed in clicks, and the property bar says what to click next. While the last point is wanted, the dimension follows the pointer. Esc starts again. Points snap as drawing does, so snapping to nodes or objects gives exact measures; see Snapping. The new dimension is selected. Parallel The Parallel Dimension tool measures the straight distance between two points, at any angle: Drag from the first point to the second, or click both. Move the pointer and click where the dimension line goes. Horizontal or Vertical The Horizontal or Vertical Dimension tool measures only the horizontal or the vertical distance between two points, whichever is larger. Place it as a parallel dimension. Angular The Angular Dimension tool measures an angle: Click the vertex of the angle. Click a point on the first side, then a point on the second side. Click where the arc goes. The angle is measured counterclockwise from the first side. Segment The Segment Dimension tool measures a segment of an object: click the segment to take its two ends, then click where the dimension line goes. Dimension style The property bar shows these settings with the dimension tools and when the selection is all dimensions. Changes apply to the selected dimensions and to the next ones you make. Precision: 0 to 6 decimals (2 at first). Units: the drawing units (at first) or any other unit. Lengths follow the drawing scale, so at 1:100 a 10 mm line reads 1000 mm; see Document options. Show units: the unit after the number (the degree sign for angles). Prefix and Suffix: text before and after the number. Text: above the line (at first), in the line, or below the line. Label size: 1 to 500 points (10 at first). The label always reads left to right and stays upright. Callout The 3-Point Callout tool draws a label with a leader line in two segments. Drag from the tip (what the callout points at) to the elbow, or click both. Click where the text goes. The text goes on that side of the elbow. Type the text. The sample text is selected, so typing replaces it. The leader always ends at the text: when you type more, change the size or move the text on its own (Ctrl+click it), the leader follows. Move the tip or the elbow with the Shape tool. The property bar, shown with the tool and when the selection is all callouts, sets: the outline width of the leader and shape (a hairline at first); the line style; the head at the tip (an arrow at first, or none); the callout shape around the text: none (at first), underline, rectangle, rounded rectangle or ellipse; the gap between the text and the leader or shape (1 mm at first).

h: Anchors Drawing a connector Connector settings Staying attached Editing anchors
x: Connector lines and anchors Connector lines join two objects and stay attached to them: when you move or resize the objects, the connector follows. They are useful for diagrams, flowcharts and organization charts. Anchors A connector attaches to an anchor of each object. Every object has four anchors, at the middle of each side of its bounding box. You can add your own anchors with the Edit Anchor tool; they move and scale with the object. Drawing a connector Three tools in the Connector flyout draw connectors: Straight-Line Connector: a straight line; Right-Angle Connector: horizontal and vertical segments with square corners; Rounded Right-Angle Connector: the same with rounded corners. To join two objects: Choose a connector tool. Drag from one object to the other. While you drag, the anchors of both objects show, and the line starts at the anchor that will be used. Release on the other object. When you start or end the drag on an anchor, that anchor is used; otherwise the closest pair of anchors of the two objects is used. The connector is an open line with no fill and the default outline. Connector settings The property bar, shown with the connector tools and when the selection is all connectors, has the three kinds of connector (with connectors selected, they change how those run), the corner radius of rounded connectors (3 mm at first), and the outline width, style and arrowheads of the selected connectors. Staying attached When you move, scale or reshape the joined objects, the connector runs again between their anchors. When you move the connector together with its objects, it stays attached. When you move the connector on its own, it lets go and becomes a plain line. Undo attaches it again. When one of its objects is deleted, the connector stays where it is. Editing anchors The Edit Anchor tool adds, moves and deletes anchors: Choose the Edit Anchor tool and click an object. Its anchors show as diamonds. Click inside the object to add an anchor there. Drag an anchor you added to move it. Select an anchor and press Delete, double-click it, or click Delete anchor on the property bar to remove it. Remove all custom anchors removes every anchor you added. The four anchors at the middle of the sides cannot be removed.

h: The Pick tool Moving, resizing and turning Dragging with the right button The property bar Selection groups The Freehand Pick tool
x: Selecting objects Before you change an object, you select it. The Pick tool (Space switches to it from most tools) selects, moves and resizes objects; the Freehand Pick tool does the same but selects with a freehand loop. The Pick tool Click an object to select it. A filled object counts where it is filled; an unfilled one on its outline. Text, groups, tables and pictures count anywhere inside their box. Shift+click adds an object to the selection or takes it out. Drag around objects, starting on an empty spot: the objects wholly inside the dashed frame are selected. Hold Alt as you finish the drag to select every object the frame touches. Hold Shift to add to the selection, Ctrl to keep the frame square. Ctrl+click selects an object inside a group, one level further in at each click. Its handles are round, and changes act on it alone. Alt+click selects the object beneath the selected one, to reach objects that are covered. Tab and Shift+Tab select the next or previous object. Esc selects nothing. Edit > Select All and a double-click on the tool's button select every object; Select All also selects all text, guidelines or nodes. The selected objects show eight square handles around them and a small cross in the middle. The status bar says what is selected and on which layer. Moving, resizing and turning Drag a selected object, or the cross in its middle, to move it. Hold Ctrl to move only horizontally or vertically. The object snaps to what snapping is set to. Drag a corner handle to resize in proportion, a side handle to stretch in one direction. Hold Shift to resize from the center, Ctrl to resize in steps of 100% (crossing the other side mirrors the object), Alt to resize freely. Click a selected object again to show the rotation handles: drag a curved corner arrow to rotate, a side arrow to skew. Hold Ctrl for steps of 15 degrees. Drag the ring in the middle to turn about another point; double-click it to put it back in the middle. While dragging, press Space or click the right button to leave a copy where the objects were; Esc cancels the drag. The arrow keys nudge the selection by the nudge distance (2.54 mm at first), with Shift by the super nudge distance and with Ctrl by the micro nudge distance. Set them on the Rulers page of the document options. + duplicates the selection in place. Dragging with the right button Drag a selected object with the right mouse button. When you release, a menu offers to move it there, copy it there, copy its fill, outline or all its properties to the object under the pointer, or place it inside that object as a clip frame. The property bar With nothing selected, the property bar shows the page size and orientation, the drawing units and the nudge distance. With a selection, it shows the position (X and Y), the size (W and H), the scale, the rotation angle, the mirror buttons, the outline width, to front and to back, and convert to curves. Text adds the text settings, and bitmaps the bitmap commands. With several objects, a group or a curve of several parts, it adds group, ungroup, combine, break apart, the shaping commands and the Align and Distribute panel. Selection groups Press Ctrl and a number from 0 to 9 to remember the selection under that number. Press the number alone to select those objects again, and again to zoom to them. Alt and the number add the selection to the group. Groups are saved with the drawing. The Freehand Pick tool The Freehand Pick tool works like the Pick tool, but a drag from an empty spot draws a loop. When you release, every object wholly inside the loop is selected; hold Alt as you release to select every object the loop touches, Shift to add to the selection. Hold Ctrl to draw a rectangle instead. The options of the Pick tool, such as whether a frame selects the objects it touches, are on the Pick page of the tool options; see Tool options.

h: The Transformations panel Position Rotate Scale and Mirror Size Skew The Free Transform tool Undoing transformations The Coordinates panel
x: Moving, scaling, rotating and skewing You can transform objects by dragging them with the Pick tool (see Selecting objects), by typing values on the property bar, with the Free Transform tool, or precisely with the Transformations panel. The Transformations panel Open the panel with Object > Transformations, or with Alt+F7 (Position), Alt+F8 (Rotate), Alt+F9 (Scale and Mirror) and Alt+F10 (Size). The buttons at the top choose one of five pages.  Every page ends with the reference point, a 3 by 3 grid that chooses the point of the selection that is placed, turned about or kept still (the center at first), Copies and Apply. Distances are in the drawing units, angles in degrees (counterclockwise), scales in percent. To transform the selection: Choose a page and type the values. Choose the reference point. Set Copies: 0 changes the selection itself; a number above 0 leaves the selection as it is and adds that many copies, each transformed once more than the one before. The copies are one undo step, and the last copy becomes the selection, so another Apply goes on from there. Click Apply. Position X and Y move the selection. With Relative position on (at first), they are a distance to move by; off, they are where the reference point goes, counted from the ruler origin. With Relative position on, the grid picks a direction: a side or a corner sets the distance to the selection's size, so each copy lands right next to the last one. Rotate Type the angle, and the Center to turn about. With Relative center on (at first), the center is counted from the reference point; off, from the ruler origin. Scale and Mirror X and Y scale in percent (100% at first). Mirror horizontally and Mirror vertically flip the selection. Proportional keeps both scales the same. Size W and H set the width and height of the selection. Proportional keeps the proportions. Skew X and Y slant the selection by angles. With Use anchor point on, the reference point stays still; off, the center does. The Free Transform tool The Free Transform tool, in the Pick flyout, transforms the selection about the point where you press. Choose a mode on the property bar: Free rotation (at first): turns the selection around the press point. Free angle reflection: mirrors the selection across the line from the press point to the pointer; moving the pointer turns that line. Free scale: scales about the press point. Free skew: horizontal movement skews horizontally, vertical movement vertically. Hold Alt to scale, Ctrl to skew or Shift to reflect for one drag, whatever the mode. With Apply to duplicate on, the press makes a copy and the drag transforms the copy, leaving the original as it was. The property bar also has the position, size, scale, angle and mirror fields. Undoing transformations Object > Clear Transformations takes the selected objects back to how they were before they were scaled, rotated or skewed. The Coordinates panel The Coordinates panel draws an object from typed coordinates, or reshapes the selected one, with a dashed preview on the drawing. Open it from Window > Panels.  Choose the kind of object with the buttons at the top: rectangle or square, ellipse or circle, polygon or regular polygon, star, complex star, 2-point line or multipoint curve. Type its values: rectangles and ellipses: the position of the origin point (chosen in a 3 by 3 grid), the width and height, the angle of rotation, and the corners of the bounding box while the angle is 0; squares and circles: the position, the side or diameter and the angle; polygons and stars: the number of points or sides, the sharpness, the angle and the circle the points lie on; regular polygons: the number of sides, the length of a side, the angle and the center; 2-point lines: the start point and end point, or the length and angle; multipoint curves: the list of points, with buttons to add and delete points and to close the curve. Instead of typing, click a button with a pointer and target, then click or drag on the drawing to set that value. A right click cancels. Click Create object to add it, or Replace object to reshape the selected rectangle, ellipse, polygon or curve while keeping its fill, outline, name and place. Positions are counted from the ruler origin, in the drawing units.

h: Aligning Distributing
x: Aligning and distributing objects Aligning lines objects up by their edges or centers; distributing spaces them evenly. Use the Align and Distribute panel (Ctrl+Shift+A), the commands of Object > Align and Distribute, or the keys below.  Aligning Select the objects. Select the one the others should line up with last. In the Align part of the panel, choose Align to: Active object (at first): the object selected last; with one object selected, the page; Page edge: the edges of the page; Page center: the center of the page; Grid: each object to the nearest line of the document grid. Click one of the six buttons: left edges, centers on a vertical line, right edges, top edges, centers on a horizontal line, or bottom edges. Use outline: align the outer edges of the outlines: with this on, the outer edges of the outlines meet, instead of the paths themselves. The keys always align to the object selected last: L Align Left R Align Right T Align Top B Align Bottom E Align Centers Horizontally C Align Centers Vertically P Center to Page Distributing Select three or more objects (two or more to distribute across the page). In the Distribute part, choose Distribute to: Selection extent (at first): the first and last objects stay where they are, and the others move between them; Page extent: the objects spread across the whole page, the first touching one side and the last the other. Click one of the eight buttons: left edges, centers, gaps or right edges across the page, or top edges, centers, gaps or bottom edges down it. Spreading the gaps gives equal space between the objects whatever their sizes. With too few objects the buttons are pale and the panel says how many are needed. Each align or distribute is one undo step. To place copies at even distances in one step, see Step and repeat.

h: To make copies
x: Making copies with Step and Repeat The Step and Repeat panel makes several copies of the selection, each moved by the same distance from the one before: a row of buttons, a column of lines, a grid of tiles. Open it with Edit > Step and Repeat (Ctrl+Shift+D).  To make copies Select the objects to copy. Set the number of Number of copies (1 to 999). Under Horizontal settings, choose how the copies are spaced across: Offset: the distance from one copy to the next, measured from the same point of each; Spacing: the gap between one copy and the next, so the copies never overlap whatever their size. Then type the distance. 0 keeps the copies in line. Do the same under Vertical settings. Click Apply. The copies are added to the active layer. Distances are in the drawing units. To copy with a rotation or a scale at each step, use the Copies field of the Transformations panel; see Moving, scaling, rotating and skewing.

h: The Objects panel Layers Master layers Renaming objects and layers Changing the order Grouping and combining Locking and hiding objects
x: Organizing objects and layers The Objects panel shows how the current page is organized: its layers, the objects on each layer, the groups and the master layers that appear on every page. Use it to select, name, hide, lock and order objects and layers. Objects higher in the list are drawn in front.  The Objects panel The panel lists the page with its layers, topmost first, then the Master Page with the master layers, the guidelines (Guides) and the Document Grid. Each object shows a swatch of its fill framed in its outline color, and its name, or what it is when it has none ("Rectangle", "Curve with 8 nodes"). Click an object to select it; Shift+click adds it to the selection. Its layer becomes the active layer. Click the arrow of a group to see the objects inside it. Each layer has three buttons: Show/hide, Print and export the layer and Lock layer. A hidden or locked layer cannot be edited. The padlock of Guides locks all the guidelines of the page. Hidden objects show their name dimmed. Layers A layer is a sheet on which objects lie. The active layer, shown in bold with a colored bar, is where new objects go when you draw, paste, duplicate or import. Click a layer to make it active. New Layer, at the bottom of the panel, adds a layer on top and makes it active. Right-click a layer for Rename, Move up, Move down and Delete layer. A page always keeps one layer. Delete at the bottom of the panel deletes the selected objects, or the active layer when nothing is selected. Master layers Objects on a master layer appear on every page, under the page's own layers: use them for a logo, a header or page numbers. Click the New Master Layer (All Pages); right-click for odd or even pages button to add one for all pages; right-click it to add one for odd or even pages only. A master layer's menu has Show on to choose All pages, Odd pages or Even pages. You can select and edit master objects from any page they show on. Renaming objects and layers Double-click a layer or an object in the panel, or choose Rename from its menu, to open the Rename Layer or Rename Object dialog box. Type the new name and click OK. An object with an empty name shows what it is again. Double-click the page row to rename the page.  Names help you find objects in the panel and in Find and replace, and are kept in exported SVG files. Changing the order Object > Order moves the selected objects: To Front of Page, To Back of Page, To Front of Layer, To Back of Layer, Forward One, Back One, In Front Of, Behind (click the object to go in front of or behind) and Reverse Order. Grouping and combining Object > Group > Group (Ctrl+G) makes the selection one group that moves and resizes together. Ungroup (Ctrl+U) splits it again, and Ungroup All also splits the groups inside it. To edit an object inside a group without ungrouping, Ctrl+click it. Combine (Ctrl+L) makes the selected objects one curve of several parts, with one fill and outline; where the parts overlap, holes appear. Break Apart (Ctrl+K) splits a curve into its parts. Convert to Curves (Ctrl+Q) turns a rectangle, ellipse, polygon or text into a curve you can edit node by node. Locking and hiding objects Object > Lock > Lock Object keeps the selected objects from being selected or changed; Unlock Object and Unlock All Objects release them. Object > Hide > Hide Object hides the selected objects; Show All Objects shows them again. To keep objects out of the way while you work on others, see also Focus mode.

h: With objects selected With nothing selected
x: The Properties panel The Properties panel (Alt+Enter) shows and changes the properties of the selected objects: their outline, fill, transparency and more, depending on what is selected. It is open at first, beside Hints and Objects. Open it again with Object > Properties.  With objects selected The top of the panel names the selected object (and how many more are selected) and gives its position and size. Under it, a row of buttons opens and closes each section the object has: QR code, for a QR code: its content and look; see Barcodes and QR codes. Outline: color, width, paint, caps, corners, dashes, arrowheads and more; see Setting outlines. Fill: the kind of fill and its settings; see Fills. F11 opens this section. Transparency: how much of what lies below shows through; see Transparency. Rectangle, for rectangles: the corner settings; see Corners. FX: the bitmap effects applied to the object; see Bitmap effects. Character, for text: the font, size, Bold and Italic, and a button to Edit with the Text tool (F8). Summary: a summary of the object. The sections you closed stay closed the next time. A change applies to every selected object and is one undo step. With nothing selected With nothing selected, the panel says No objects selected and shows the Default properties for new objects: the fill and outline that new shapes and lines get. Change them here to draw with other colors from the start. See Object styles and defaults.

h: To place objects inside a frame Editing what is inside Opacity masks Empty frames
x: Placing objects inside a frame A clip frame is a closed object that holds other objects and shows only the parts of them that lie inside it, like a picture in a window. The frame keeps its own fill and outline; the objects inside stay whole and can be taken out again. The commands are in Object > Clip to Frame. To place objects inside a frame Select the objects to place inside. Choose Object > Clip to Frame > Place Inside Frame. Click the closed object that will be the frame. The objects keep their position. You can also drag the objects onto the frame with the right mouse button and choose to place them inside; see Dragging with the right button. Editing what is inside Edit Contents enters the frame: only the objects inside can be edited, the rest of the page is dimmed and the frame shows as an outline. Finish Editing Contents, or the button on the property bar, leaves it. Extract Contents makes the objects inside ordinary objects again; the frame stays, empty. Lock Contents to Frame (on at first): moving, scaling or rotating the frame takes the contents along. Turned off, the frame moves alone and the contents stay where they are on the page. Double-clicking a frame with the Pick tool also enters it; see Focus mode. Opacity masks Object > Clip to Frame > Opacity Mask turns the selected clip frames into opacity masks: the frame is no longer drawn, and its brightness decides how much of the contents shows: fully where it is white, not at all where it is black, and nothing outside the frame. Fill the frame with a gradient for a soft fade. Invert Mask swaps that, so black shows. Choose the command again to turn the mask back into a plain frame. Empty frames Right-click an object and use its frame type commands: Create empty clip frame turns each selected object into an empty clip frame, ready to hold objects. No frame turns an empty clip frame back into the object it was. Create empty text frame replaces the object by an empty paragraph text frame of its size, ready for the Text tool. Cropping a bitmap with the Crop tool or the Shape tool also places it in a clip frame; see Cropping, cutting and erasing.

h: To create a symmetry Editing a symmetry Removing or keeping the copies
x: Drawing with symmetry Symmetry draws live mirrored copies of an object across one or more mirror lines. The copies follow every change you make to the original, so you draw one half (or one slice) and see the whole. The commands are in Object > Symmetry. To create a symmetry Select an object. Choose Object > Symmetry > Create New Symmetry (Alt+S). A vertical mirror line is placed at the right edge of the object, so the copy appears next to it, and TraceDraw goes straight into editing the symmetry. Editing a symmetry Edit Symmetry (Alt+E) edits the symmetry of the selected object. The original is outlined in red, and a bar at the top left of the drawing window sets: the number of mirror lines, 1 to 12, spread evenly around the center. With more lines you get a kaleidoscope: with n lines there are 2*n* - 1 copies; the center (X and Y); the angle of the first line (0 to 360 degrees). Edit the original as usual, with any tool; the copies follow. While an object with symmetry is selected, its mirror lines show as dashed lines. Click Finish on the bar, or choose Finish Editing Symmetry (Alt+Shift+E), to stop editing. Removing or keeping the copies Remove Symmetry (Alt+Shift+S) removes the symmetry; the copies go away. Break Symmetry Link (Alt+X) turns the copies into objects of their own, which no longer follow the original.

h: Entering and leaving focus mode While in focus mode Settings
x: Focus mode Focus mode lets you edit the objects inside a group or a clip frame without ungrouping it, with the rest of the drawing faded behind it. Entering and leaving focus mode Double-click a group or a clip frame with the Pick tool. Or right-click an object and choose Bring into focus. For an object inside a group, the group gets the focus and the object stays selected. Double-click a group inside the focused group to go one level deeper. Press Esc with nothing selected to go up one level, and leave focus mode from the top. The cross on the breadcrumb bar leaves at once. While in focus mode A bar at the top left of the drawing window shows the name of the drawing, then each group on the way down. Click a step to go back to that group, or the name of the drawing to leave focus mode. Clicks and marquees select the objects inside the focused group, so you can move, color or delete them with the Pick tool as usual. Everything else is faded. Exports and printing are not affected. Settings How faded the other objects are is set by the visibility of inactive objects (0 to 100%, 20% at first) on the Edit page of Tools > Options > TraceDraw. Whether a double-click enters focus mode is set on the same page. See TraceDraw options.

h: Making a symbol Placing instances Turning instances back into objects
x: Symbols A symbol is an object you define once and place many times. Each copy, called an instance, is a link to the definition: edit the definition and every instance changes. Symbols keep files small and repeated parts the same. They are listed in the Symbols panel (Ctrl+F3).  Making a symbol Select the objects that make up the symbol. Click New symbol from selection in the Symbols panel, or choose Object > Symbol > New Symbol or Object > Create > Symbol. The selection becomes the first instance of the new symbol. Placing instances The panel lists the symbols of the drawing, each with the number of its instances. Click Insert beside a symbol to place a new instance, or choose Object > Symbol > Insert Symbol. Instances can be moved, scaled and turned like any object. Turning instances back into objects Select instances and click Revert to objects, or choose Object > Symbol > Revert to Objects. They become ordinary objects that no longer follow the symbol.

h: Adding and editing data
x: Object data The Object Data panel attaches your own information to an object, as named fields: a part number, a price, a note. The data is saved with the drawing and goes with the object when you copy it.  Adding and editing data Select an object. With nothing selected, the panel says Select an object.. The panel lists the object's fields in two columns, Field and Value. Click a name or a value to edit it. Click Add field to add a field, or one of the buttons for a common field: Name, Cost, Comments and CDRStaticID. Click the x at the end of a row to remove the field. When the selected objects have a Cost field with a number, the panel shows their total cost. Some features keep their own data in objects, such as dimension lines, callouts, connectors and anchors; you rarely need to change those fields by hand.

h: To add a link Bookmarks Links in exported files
x: Links and bookmarks The Links and Bookmarks panel gives objects a hyperlink, so a click on them in an exported PDF, SVG or web page opens a web address, writes an email or goes to another page. It also lists the named objects of the drawing as bookmarks. Open it from Window > Panels.  To add a link Select one or more objects. Type the address in the Hyperlink field and leave the field. The buttons Web, E-mail and Page put https://, mailto: or #page= in front of the text, so for a page link you only type its number. Click Remove to take a link away, or empty the field. Bookmarks Under Bookmarks (named objects), the panel lists one button per object that has a name. Click one to select the object and zoom to it. To name objects, see Renaming objects and layers. Links in exported files In PDF files, each linked object becomes a clickable area over its box. A page link goes to the top of that page of the file. PDF/X files get no links, as those standards do not allow them. In SVG and web pages, the object itself is the link. A link on a group covers all its objects; the links of the objects inside are left out.

h: To paste in another form
x: Paste Special Edit > Paste Special chooses how the content of the clipboard comes into the drawing, when it could come in more than one way: for example text copied from another program can become a text object, and an SVG copied from a web page can become editable shapes or a picture.  To paste in another form Copy something, in TraceDraw or in another program. Choose Edit > Paste Special. Under Paste as, choose one of the forms the clipboard offers: Objects (internal clipboard): objects copied in TraceDraw, as they were; Vector objects (SVG text): SVG text, turned into shapes you can edit; Bitmap: an image, as a bitmap; Artistic text: plain text, as a line of text. Click OK. When the clipboard holds nothing that can be pasted, the dialog box says The clipboard is empty. The ordinary Paste (Ctrl+V) pastes in the first form available, and Paste in View (Ctrl+Shift+V) pastes in the middle of the window.

h: Adding to the Shelf Placing an item Arranging items Removing an item Where the Shelf is kept
x: The Shelf The Shelf panel keeps objects and colors apart from any drawing, so you can place them in this drawing or another one, today or after TraceDraw restarts: logos, stamps, frames, a set of colors. Open it from Window > Panels, or right-click a selection and choose Add to Shelf.  Adding to the Shelf Select objects and click Add Selection. The item is named after the object (its name, or what it is), or "n objects". Symbols become plain objects, and the object styles they use go along. Click Add Colours to keep the colors of the drawing's document palette and its color styles as one item. The Shelf holds up to 500 items. Placing an item Drag an item onto the drawing to place a copy under the pointer. Double-click an item, or choose it and click Place, to place a copy in the middle of the view. The copies go on the active layer and are selected; one undo removes them. A color item adds its colors to the document palette and its color styles to the drawing. Arranging items Click an item to choose it. Right-click it for Place, Rename and Remove. Drag an item onto another to move it to that place. Removing an item Choose an item and click Remove. Removing cannot be undone, so TraceDraw asks first: click Remove to confirm or Cancel to keep it. Tick Do not ask again to remove items without asking; to be asked again, turn on Before an item is removed from the Shelf on the Warnings page of the global options.  Where the Shelf is kept On the desktop, the Shelf is a file in your preferences folder. In the browser, it is kept in that browser's storage, which holds only a few megabytes, so large bitmaps may not be kept.

h: Finding and replacing text Finding objects
x: Finding and replacing The Find and Replace panel (Ctrl+F) finds text in the drawing, and replaces it, or finds objects by name. Open it with Edit > Find and Replace.  Finding and replacing text Choose Text. Type what to look for in Find, and the new text in Replace with. Tick Match case to tell capitals from small letters, and Whole words only to skip the text when it is part of a longer word. Click Find Next to select the next text object that holds it, or Find All to select them all. Click Replace to replace it in the selected text, or Replace All to replace it everywhere. The panel says how many were found. Finding objects Choose Objects, type part of a name, or a kind of object such as "Rectangle", and click Find Next or Find All. The search covers the current page. To name objects, see Renaming objects and layers.

h: Adding a comment Reading and answering
x: Comments The Comments panel collects review notes on a drawing: pins, boxes and arrows on the page, each with a text and replies. Comments are saved with the drawing (in .tdraw files) and are never printed or exported. Open the panel from Window > Panels.  Adding a comment Type your name in Name. It signs your comments and replies. Left empty, the author of the drawing is used. Next to Add, click Pin, Box or Arrow. On the page, click to place a pin, or drag to draw a box around something or an arrow pointing at it. Type the comment. Each comment shows its number in an orange bubble on the page. Reading and answering The panel lists the comments, with how many are open, each with its number, author, date and time, page, text and replies. Click a card to choose the comment and go to its page; with the panel open, you can also click a bubble or a box on the page. Edit the text of the chosen comment, or type in the Reply field and press Enter or click Reply. Resolve marks a comment as dealt with; Reopen opens it again. Resolved comments are hidden unless Show resolved is ticked. Hide marks hides the bubbles, boxes and arrows on the page. Delete removes a comment and its replies. Every change is one undo step. Deleting a page deletes its comments.
